---
title: "CVD case fatality"
description: "How BNR measures death before discharge following a hospital-registered CVD event."
---

In-hospital case fatality is the percentage of eligible hospital-registered CVD events where the patient died before discharge.

## At a glance

| Element | Description |
|---|---|
| **Question answered** | What proportion of eligible hospital CVD events ended in death before discharge? |
| **Numerator** | Eligible events ending in a confirmed in-hospital death |
| **Denominator** | Eligible hospital events with a known discharge outcome |
| **Reported as** | Percentage |
| **Unit** | Hospital-registered event |

## What does this measure tell us?

Case fatality describes short-term outcome among people reaching the hospital-event series. It is not the same as a population mortality rate: its denominator is a group of CVD events, not the general population.

## How do we calculate it?

$$
\text{Case fatality (\%)} = \frac{\text{in-hospital deaths}}{\text{eligible events with known outcome}} \times 100
$$

BNR may also show a clearly labelled sensitivity estimate that combines confirmed deaths with probable deaths. This is useful when recent discharge outcomes remain incomplete, but it must remain distinguishable from the confirmed measure.

## What is included and excluded?

The measure includes eligible hospital-registered heart attack or stroke events among Barbados residents. Death-certificate-only records, duplicates, non-residents and events without the outcome information required for the chosen estimate are excluded from the confirmed measure.

When BNR reports a probable-death sensitivity series, the publication states the time rule used and explains why it was needed.

## Worked example

If 12 confirmed in-hospital deaths occurred among 150 eligible events with a known discharge outcome:

$$
\frac{12}{150} \times 100 = 8\%
$$

The in-hospital case fatality would be **8%**.

## How should it be interpreted?

A lower percentage can indicate improved survival, but comparisons also depend on age, severity, event mix, access to hospital care, transfers and completeness of outcome recording. Age-adjusted estimates may be used to improve comparisons across periods or groups.

## Things to bear in mind

- Case fatality describes deaths among eligible hospital events, not deaths in the whole population.
- Confirmed and confirmed-plus-probable series should not be treated as identical.
- Recent periods may change as outcomes are completed.
- Small numerators and denominators can produce unstable percentages.
